summary: This excerpt from a novel (labeled Book 11, part 32) describes life in the Pleasant River villages of Riverboro. It opens with Abner Simpson's account of being cheated by a red-haired, hare-lipped stranger who swapped a sleigh for an old cider press and took four dollars and seventy-five cents, which the sheriff mocks. It then sketches the Simpson household's hardships and how the village's quiet, idle hours fuel gossip, using Delia Weeks, who left Riverboro for Lewiston, as an example of someone who resented being watched.
one_line: A Riverboro excerpt where Abner Simpson is swindled by a stranger in a sleigh-for-cider-press trade, and village gossip is examined through Delia Weeks.
key_facts: Abner Simpson avowed his complete innocence after being swindled in a trade.
A red-haired man with a hare lip and a pepper-and-salt suit offered to swap Abner a good sleigh for an old cider press.
Abner paid the hare-lipped stranger four dollars and seventy-five cents to boot.
The stranger set down the sleigh, took the cider press on his cart, and vanished up the road.
Abner said that if he could catch the thief he would make him dance.
The sheriff told Abner he would never catch the man, since nobody had ever seen the stranger but Abner.
Mrs. Simpson, Abner's wife, took in washing and went out to do days' cleaning.
The town helped feed and clothe the Simpson children.
George, a lanky boy of fourteen, did chores on neighboring farms.
The Simpson children included Samuel, Clara Belle, Susan, Elijah, and Elisha, who attended school when sufficiently clothed.
Village conversation took place under the trees at noon, hanging over the bridge at nightfall, and around the stove in the village store.
Delia Weeks was a maiden lady who did dressmaking in a small way.
Delia Weeks fell into a decline before her cousin Cyrus asked her to keep house for him in Lewiston.
In a year in Lewiston, Delia grew into a robust, hearty, cheerful woman.
Delia said she was 'bein' worn to a shadder' in Riverboro trying to keep her secrets to herself and never succeeding.
